metadata.title: Safety Testing of Human Allogeneic Cells Expanded for Use in Cell-Based Medical Products

Allogeneic cells of human origin may be expanded in culture to manufacture medical products 17 consisting of live cells, inactivated cells, cell lysates, or other cell-based materials such as cell- 18 derived particles. We, FDA, are providing you, sponsors of allogeneic cell-based medical 19 products, recommendations for determining the appropriate cell safety testing to support an 20 Investigational New Drug Application (IND) 1 or a Biologics License Application (BLA). 2 Cell 21 safety testing should be based on a risk analysis that considers the expansion potential of the 22 cells, the reagents that are used to expand the cells in culture, and the number of individuals the 23 cell-based medical product is capable of treating. 3 , 4

candidates.context: Viral and microbial contamination is a potential risk for all cell-based medical products, 59 especially when the cells are cultured extensively during manufacturing. Contamination may be 60 present in the source cells, or the cells may become contaminated with adventitious agents 61 during manufacturing. In addition, genomic changes that result in tumorigenic cells can occur 62 during extensive culture. 63 (i) Identified by history; 68

candidates.statement: In addition, 21 CFR 312.23(a)(7)(i) requires an IND to include sufficient information to assure 73 the proper identification, quality, purity, and strength of the investigational product. An IND is 74 also specifically required to include a description of the acceptable limits and analytical methods 75 used to assure, among other things, the purity and quality of both the drug substance (DS) and 76 drug product (DP), 21 CFR 312.23(a)(7)(iv)(a)-(b). Potential impurities for cell-based medical 77 products include contamination with viruses or bacteria. Genomic integrity and in vitro growth 78 characteristics are factors that affect the quality of cell-based medical products used under INDs 79 and thus should be evaluated. FDA may place an IND on clinical hold if the IND does not 80 contain sufficient CMC information required under 21 CFR 312.23 “to assess the risks to 81 subjects of the proposed studies” (21 CFR 312.42(b)(1)(iv) and (b)(2)(i)) or if the CMC 82 information indicates that the “[h]uman subjects are or would be exposed to an unreasonable and 83 significant risk of illness or injury” (21 CFR 312.42(b)(1)(i) and (b)(2)(i)). 84

candidates.statement: Cell banks made from continuous cell lines should be tested for adventitious viruses and 129 undergo additional safety evaluations as outlined in section V of this guidance. 130
candidates.context: Cellular products may be produced from continuous cell lines, including induced 123 pluripotent stem cells, embryonic stem cells, cancer cell lines, and transformed cell lines. 124 The manufacturing process for a cellular product made from continuous cell lines usually 125 includes the creation of a cell bank to ensure a consistent source material for the 126 manufacture of the cell-based product. 127

candidates.statement: If allogeneic primary cells from a single donor can be expanded in culture to a cell 136 number that is sufficient to be administered to many individuals, then we recommend 137 conducting the cell safety testing described in section V of this guidance. This testing 138 should generally be performed on a cryopreserved cell bank. However, some 139 manufacturers of cell-based medical products do not use a cell bank during 140 manufacturing. Instead, they expand the cells extensively and then store them as a 141 cryopreserved lot of drug substance or final product. In this case, the cell safety 142 testing outlined in section V of this guidance should be done on the lot of 143 cryopreserved cells. 144

candidates.statement: Primary cell cultures that are not subcultivated or primary cell cultures that are 158 subsequently subcultivated for only a very limited number of population doublings are 159 not subject to the provisions in 21 CFR 610.18(c) for cell lines used for manufacturing 160 biological products (21 CFR 610.18(c)(3)). It is not recommended that primary 161 allogeneic cells that are minimally expanded in culture to be administered to only a few 162 individuals, or a single individual, undergo cytogenetic analysis or adventitious virus 163 testing. However, these cells must still be tested for sterility (21 CFR 610.12), purity 164 (e.g., endotoxin) (21 CFR 610.13), as required for lot release of licensed cellular products 165 (21 CFR 610.1). Note that if there are specific safety concerns regarding reagents used 166 during product manufacturing, then adventitious virus testing may need to be performed 167 on the reagents of concern to assure product safety. For example, there may be a safety 168 concern due to the use of animal and human derived reagents because they have the 169 potential to introduce adventitious agents to the cell-based medical product. 170

candidates.statement: Some manufacturing schemes may use multiple levels of cell banks; however, it may not be 183 necessary to test all the cell banks for safety as outlined below. For instance, cells used as the 184 cellular starting material for genetically engineered stem cells may be banked but would not be 185 considered the MCB. Instead, the cell bank of genetically modified stem cells would generally 186 be considered the MCB, and the cell safety testing described below should be performed on 187 those genetically modified cells since there is potential for adventitious agent contamination 188 during the genetic modification. Likewise, if donor cells used as starting material for a cell- 189 based product are banked prior to extensive expansion in culture, the highly expanded cells 190 should be considered the MCB and should be used for the safety testing outlined below. 191
candidates.context: Cell-based medical products may use a one-tier or two-tier cell banking system. A one-tier 179 system consists of a master cell bank (MCB) only, while in a two-tier system there is also at least 180 one working cell bank (WCB) derived from the MCB. 181 Some cell-based medical products do not use a cell bank during manufacturing but may store the 193 final product as a single lot of highly expanded cryopreserved cells that could be used to treat 194 many individuals. candidates.statement: • In vitro adventitious virus testing – Three cell lines should generally be used: 222 human diploid (e.g., MRC5 cells), monkey kidney (e.g., Vero cells), and 223 another cell line of the same species and tissue type as that used for 224 production (e.g., HeLa cells if the product was made using human cells). 225 However, different cell lines may be appropriate depending on the 226 manufacturing process. In this example, testing for adventitious viruses using BHK21 229 cells would address the recommendation of testing for viruses in cells of the 230 same species in which product production occurs.
